newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Poor nations say they get no help for conservation.
newsitem.headline: Poor nations say they get no help for conservation.

text.p: The Group of 77 developing nations and China on Wednesday blamed rich countries for the world's poor track record on protecting the environment.

Presenting their final statement at a conference in Argentina, they said rich nations had broken their promise to pick up the tab for conservation efforts under the 1992 Convention on Biological Diversity.

"Developed countries are hindering implementation of the convention and at the same time they are not permitting developing countries to comply with their commitments," Costa Rican Environment Minister Rene Castro said.

"The strong partnership we had envisaged would emerge between the North and South never really materalized. This partnership is so fragile we could say that it exists in brackets only," he added. He spoke on behalf of the G-77 and China at the Third Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biodiversity.

Rich nations agreed at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, where the convention was drafted, to provide new funds for its implemention. The convention aims to prevent any further loss of species and ecosystems around the world.
But after topping out at about $60 billion in 1992, overall overseas development aid has steadily declined.
"Any financial resources that have been made available so far could at best be described as a trickle," Castro said.

Jostling between delegations from the North and South over control of the funds has blocked a decision at the conference, which opened on Nov. 4, to appoint the so-called Global Environment Facility (GEF) as a permanent financing mechanism for the convention.
The GEF, a fund handled by the World Bank and U.N. agencies, is expected to be confirmed at the end of the conference on Friday as only an interim financing mechanism.
Ireland's Environment Minister Brendan Howlin, speaking on behalf of the European Union, urged countries to move from talk to action to bring about desired results.

"Four years later there is no doubt the threats and challenges facing biological diversity have not diminished in spite of the many efforts fostered by this convention," he said. "Decisions taken by the parties still need to be made Howlin urged countries to develop national strategies integrating biodiversity concerns into sectorial policies in time for a special session of the United Nations next June bringing the convention under review.
